prospect.name: Alan
prospect.aka: ali — the Zoom display name the diarization used throughout
prospect.occupation: Business owner in construction, with a sales team of his own — 'I'm in business. I'm a business owner. I have salespeople' and 'I'm in construction'
prospect.training_background: Trained four to five times a week at a gym previously, now once or twice a week; the gym is a three-hour round trip. Moved to CrossFit near home, which repeatedly injured his back. History of races. Recently started golf. Has cycled through workout buddies, in-person personal trainers, online personal trainers and self-directed training over six to seven years.
prospect.medical: Chronic lower back pain for approximately ten years; believes it is a degenerated disc and had an MRI a long time ago. Flare-ups cost him two to three weeks each time and recur. Takes Advil at night for the pain. Whole-body stiffness rated 10/10 on waking — neck, lower back, arms, shoulders, wrists, knees — taking about an hour to loosen. Previous plantar fasciitis. Has seen chiropractors, physical therapists and doctors. No current clinician, treatment plan or clearance mentioned.

signals: Lost ground to injury over a long stretch and wants the earlier version back — 'typically I would just push myself and I would do like, you know, part in races, other races, but now I'm just kind of like being cautious'
Visible regret at what he has become: 'I don't like that version of myself either, because now I feel like I'm getting fat' and 'this is probably the worst out of shape I've been'

Alternate reading is the_medically_constrained — high intent, explicitly no price resistance, and the blocker is a ten-year back injury the programme may not be able to work around: 'if I do one wrong kettlebell, the consequence of that is like back pain for three weeks'

Second alternate is skeptical_bargain_hunter — he holds a $200/month cancellable subscription as the reference point — but he ruled price out himself: 'I've wasted millions of dollars. I don't give a about six grand. It's about my own personal commitment.'

goals.text: Lose the fat, get ripped and finally have a cut six-pack — 'I want to have a body like Trevor's'
A physique he is proud of; he has only ever had 'a little baby six-pack'
A simple 20-40 minute routine he can do at home with one kettlebell instead of a three-hour round trip to the gym
Get rid of whole-body stiffness so he can wake without needing an hour to loosen up, and rotate properly for golf
Keep up with his 9 and 11 year olds — 'these guys are like rugrats. They run around, and I got to keep up with them'
Be spontaneous and adventurous again — jump in the ocean, climb a mountain, pick up a race
Train without triggering the back — 'how can I protect my back from, you know, not injuring myself?'
Break a six-to-seven year on-off cycle and finally master one simple thing he can keep
Show up differently in life — 'when you're in good fit and good physique, and you feel good about yourself, people see that'

pains.text: Chronic lower back pain for ten years, believed to be a degenerated disc; each flare costs two to three weeks and the cycle has repeated several times
Whole-body stiffness rated 10 out of 10 on waking, taking an hour every day to loosen up
Six to seven years of starting programmes and stopping — 'I do programs all the time, but I stop'
Gets bored and loses the reason — 'I forget why I started... then I get confused'
Has exhausted the market without resolution — chiropractors, physical therapists, doctors, MRIs, in-person and online trainers, workout buddies
Has become cautious and avoidant out of fear of re-injury, which he dislikes about himself
Frequent travel breaks the rhythm, with drinking involved — 'I go off for like two weeks, and I lose my rhythm'
The gym he likes is a three-hour round trip, which has effectively ended his attendance
Worst shape he has been in and aware his belly is growing, though only he notices
Takes painkillers at night to sleep through the back pain

objections.raw_quote: Well, I mean, I wanted to try, like, I'd rather try a session and see if, like, it's going to agitate my back or if it's going to, like, you know what mean? Like, I don't want to just pay you $6,000 and expect.
objections.rep_response: Answered with reassurance rather than assessment — 'Of course, if your back starts exploding. Yeah. We'll send it back, but that's not gonna happen' — then described the onboarding call with Trevor as the place the back would be addressed. Earlier he had offered his father's hernia as a precedent: 'he started doing cattle belts. He has had a hernia, et cetera, himself. Now he doesn't feel it anymore.' Never asked whether a clinician had cleared him.

objections.raw_quote: I think more than anything, I just need to think about it a little bit.
objections.rep_response: Ran a long think-about-it play over roughly twenty minutes — asked what specifically he needed to think about, separated thinking from excuse-making ('is it about thinking about it, or is it more so about just making an excuse to think about it?'), called back the ten-year consequence answer, and tested the exit ('Are you saying that just to get off the call with me?'). Also told him twice that he was lying to himself.

objections.raw_quote: at least over here, I was paying $200 a month, I could cancel the subscription, I'm giving you $6,000 up front, tomorrow, a month later, I have back injuries, something happens, it doesn't work out for me, you know what And then you could say, well, you dropped the ball. It's not, you know, it's very front-loaded, which is not what I'm looking for.
objections.rep_response: [proposed type: prepayment_structure_risk] Defended the front-loading as a deliberate commitment device — 'the main reason always people do pay upfront completely is because you're not just going to flake' — and offered an informal precedent for pausing: 'someone stopped working with us a couple of months ago, because he got an injury... so we just put it on pause, so it's something we can do.'

objections.raw_quote: I have like seven or eight World Cup tickets lined up in different cities. So I have a lot of traveling. We're going to be like, it's not ideal. You know what mean? Like, I'm like going on vacation mode right now. I'm not like zoned in mode right now.
objections.rep_response: Ran the never-the-right-time move: 'there's also people actually taking action when there is a World Cup, because there's never going to be the right time to actually do something. Not now, not in five years, not in 10 years, not in a hundred years.'

objections.raw_quote: my mindset is not fixed to succeed because I've failed so many times with different programs that I've done. I've had chiropractors, I've had physical therapists, I've had doctors, had MRIs, I have personal trainers... I've done it all.
objections.rep_response: Did not engage the fear directly. The prospect supplied his own learned-helplessness metaphor — the shark that stops hitting the glass — and the rep neither used it nor named the pattern; he returned to the excuse frame and to the ten-year consequence.

offer.payment_plan_terms: Offered only reactively and never structured: 'It doesn't need to be upfront. We can split it up if that's what you absolutely want. But the people who commit... six grand up front, are going to get usually the best results.'
offer.guarantee_mentioned: Two separate and informal assurances, neither with terms. On refund: 'Of course, if your back starts exploding. Yeah. We'll send it back, but that's not gonna happen.' On pausing: 'someone, like, stopped working with us a couple of months ago, because he got an injury, and he just stopped working with us again, so we just put it on pause, so it's something we can do.'

evidence: No payment, no link, no agreement and no onboarding booking; the call ended on a stated one-to-two day decision window
'just give me a day or two and I'll get back to you' and 'if I decide to move forward with you, I'll let you know as well'
The rep tested the exit and got an assurance it was genuine: 'I genuinely am thinking about it'

Counter-evidence pointing toward lost: he floated never — 'I just have to see if I want to do it today or maybe in a month from now or maybe later. Or maybe never' — and framed the whole decision as a commitment problem he has failed at repeatedly

Counter-evidence pointing toward live: price was explicitly not the obstacle ('I've wasted millions of dollars. I don't give a about six grand') and he said the presentation was good and the plan sound
outcome.next_step: Prospect to decide within one to two days and call the rep; he asked to be phoned rather than messaged. Rep also offered to book a progress check-in a month or two after starting.

notable.note: The clinical picture is the story of this call. A 41-year-old with ten years of back pain he believes is a degenerated disc, who opened by asking how he could protect his back, was taken through a full pitch for three to four loaded kettlebell sessions a week without anyone asking whether a doctor had cleared him. The rep disclaimed twice that 'we're not doctors' and then said of a back flare-up 'that's not gonna happen'. Separately, the rep only discovered at 01:07 — an hour and seven minutes in, and after the price — that the prospect was a construction business owner with his own sales team who considers $6,000 immaterial, because work was never asked about. The prospect also identified the sales process explicitly ('I love how you did your sales cycle... what you're doing to me is what we do to them') and the rep engaged with that rather than deflecting.

quality.notes: Attribution is unreliable throughout and inverts most often on short exchanges. The opening location exchange at 00:06:35 puts the rep's own answer ('I'm currently located in the Netherlands') inside the prospect's block, and the prospect's name confirmation ('Yeah, it's Alan, yeah') is merged into the rep's turn at 00:06:15. Question and answer are routinely fused — 'Six, six feet. Six feet and what's your age?' at 00:10:32 and 'I am just curious, would you be willing to settle for that?' attributed to the prospect at 00:36:47. The prospect's display label is the lowercase 'ali' while the rep addresses him as Alan for the whole call, which is why the name is recorded as Alan with the label kept in aka. Role was read from content throughout. The recording also runs from 00:00:07 to 00:06:06 with only setup audio while the prospect fought with his microphone and the rep offered to phone him.
